# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

423			// Same shape as the dirty-tree override and scoped the same way: the
424			// ONE remedy a failed session export invalidates is the one whose first
425			// stage IS that export.
426			return setupNoSessionsHint(brainCmd)
427		case h.Issues > 0 || h.Severity != "" && h.Severity != "ok":
428			return command
429		case h.HostCLIMissing && len(h.Failed) > 0:
430			return "`" + entireBinaryName + "` is not on PATH; install the Entire CLI, then run `" + brainCmd + " setup`"
431		default:
432			return command
433		}
434	}
435	
436	// Line renders the verdict.
437	func (h statusHealth) Line(render *tui.Renderer, brainCmd string) string {
438		brainCmd = base.SetupBrainCommand(brainCmd)
439		if h.Healthy() {
440			return render.Mark(tui.MarkDone) + " " + render.PhasePaint(tui.PhaseDone, "healthy")
441		}
442		parts := make([]string, 0, 6)
443		if h.BrainMissing {
444			parts = append(parts, "no brain for this repo yet")
445		}
446		if h.SemanticMissing {
447			parts = append(parts, "no code index")
448		}
449		if len(h.Failed) > 0 {
450			parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s failed", strings.Join(h.Failed, ", ")))
451		}
452		if h.Issues > 0 {
453			parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%d %s", h.Issues, plural(h.Issues, "issue")))
454		}
455		if h.Warnings > 0 {
456			parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%d %s", h.Warnings, plural(h.Warnings, "warning")))
457		}
458		if h.Severity != "" && h.Severity != "ok" {
459			parts = append(parts, "freshness "+h.Severity)
460		}
461		phase := tui.PhaseSkipped
462		mark := tui.MarkSkipped
463		if len(h.Failed) > 0 || h.Severity == "unsafe" {
464			phase = tui.PhaseFailed
465			mark = tui.MarkFailed
466		}
467		line := render.Mark(mark) + " " + render.PhasePaint(phase, strings.Join(parts, ", ")) +
468			render.Dim(" "+render.Dash()+" "+h.nextStepMessage(brainCmd))
469		if h.Cause != "" {
470			line += "\n  " + render.Dim(h.Cause)
471		}
472		return line
473	}
474	
475	func plural(n int, word string) string {
476		if n == 1 {
477			return word
478		}
479		return word + "s"
480	}
481	
482	// statusFactsIdentity renders the fact count on the identity line. A bare
483	// "5 facts" is the manifest's CLAIM, and printing it unqualified is how a
484	// brain that had lost a fact still said 5 while recall produced 4. When the
485	// cross-check fails, both numbers are shown so the claim can never be mistaken
486	// for an observation.
487	func statusFactsIdentity(f *brainStatusFacts) string {
488		if f.Integrity == nil || f.Integrity.OK() {
489			return fmt.Sprintf("memories: %d", f.Facts)
490		}
491		// A store that would not parse yielded no count at all, so "0 readable"
492		// would be a measurement nobody took. Say what is true: it could not be
493		// read.
494		if f.Integrity.Mode == factStoreDefectUnreadable {
495			return fmt.Sprintf("memories: %d declared, store unreadable", f.Facts)
496		}
497		return fmt.Sprintf("memories: %d declared, %d readable", f.Facts, f.Integrity.Readable)
498	}
499	
500	// statusLabelWidth aligns the short report's left column.
501	const statusLabelWidth = 9
502	
503	// statusBarWidth is the mini bar in the onboarding block.
504	const statusBarWidth = 14
505	
506	// renderBrainStatusShort is the DEFAULT report: who this brain is, how far
507	// onboarding has got, and one line of verdict. Everything else is one flag away.
508	func renderBrainStatusShort(out io.Writer, render *tui.Renderer, report brainStatusReport, brainCmd string) {
509		brainCmd = base.SetupBrainCommand(brainCmd)
510		// The leading and trailing blank lines separate the report from the shell
511		// prompt on both sides. The path stays in --verbose; it is machine detail.
512		fmt.Fprintln(out)
513		fmt.Fprintf(out, "%s  %s\n",
514			render.Bold(render.PhasePaint(tui.PhaseInstant, "Brain")),
515			render.Bold(valueOrUnset(report.Repo.Key)))
516		identity := []string{"manifest: " + report.Brain.ManifestState}
517		if s := report.Semantic; s != nil && s.Coverage != nil {
518			identity = append(identity, fmt.Sprintf("code index: %d files, %d symbols", s.Coverage.Files, s.Coverage.Symbols))
519		}
520		if f := report.Facts; f != nil {
521			if report.Integrity == "not_checked" {
522				identity = append(identity, fmt.Sprintf("memories: %d declared", f.Facts))
523			} else {
524				identity = append(identity, statusFactsIdentity(f))
525			}
526		}
527		if h := report.Hosted; h != nil {
528			identity = append(identity, "Brainstore: "+hostedStateLabel(h.State))
529		}
530		for _, item := range identity {
531			fmt.Fprintf(out, "  %s\n", render.Dim(item))
532		}
533	
534		if f := report.Facts; f != nil {
535			warning := ""
536			if f.Integrity != nil {
537				warning = f.Integrity.Warning()
538			} else if len(f.MissingBranches) > 0 {
539				warning = missingFactStoreWarning(f.MissingBranches)
540			}
541			if warning != "" {
542				fmt.Fprintf(out, "  %s %s\n", render.Mark(tui.MarkFailed), render.PhasePaint(tui.PhaseFailed, warning))
543			}
544		}
545	
546		// The verdict is computed BEFORE the onboarding block so the block knows
547		// which remedy the screen is already going to state. Without that, the two
548		// halves repeat each other: a dirty tree failing both seed and semantic put
549		// the same sentence on screen three times.
550		health := buildStatusHealth(report)
551		renderStatusOnboardingBlock(out, render, report, brainCmd, health.nextStepMessage(brainCmd))
552	
553		// health is already built above, deliberately before the onboarding block.
554		// main added this branch alongside a second `health :=` at this line; the
555		// declaration is dropped here rather than the one above, because the
556		// onboarding block depends on being able to read the verdict first.
557		if report.Integrity == "not_checked" && health.Healthy() {
558			fmt.Fprintf(out, "\n%s up to date\n", render.Mark(tui.MarkDone))
559		} else {
560			fmt.Fprintf(out, "\n%s\n", health.Line(render, brainCmd))
561		}
562		fmt.Fprintf(out, "%s\n", render.Dim("  `"+brainCmd+" status --verbose` for the full report"))
563		fmt.Fprintln(out)
564	}
565	
566	// renderStatusOnboardingBlock is the part a person actually came for: is the
567	// backfill moving, is the watcher alive, did every source build.
568	// stated is the remedy the verdict will print under this block; a component
569	// hint identical to it is dropped rather than said twice.
570	func renderStatusOnboardingBlock(out io.Writer, render *tui.Renderer, report brainStatusReport, brainCmd, stated string) {
571		brainCmd = base.SetupBrainCommand(brainCmd)
572		onboarding := report.Onboarding
573		if onboarding == nil {
574			return
575		}
576		fmt.Fprintf(out, "\n%s\n", render.Bold("Onboarding"))
577		// FIRST, because it decides whether any other line is ever acted on. A
578		// brain no agent knows about reads healthy on every source and is never
579		// consulted; nothing else in this report would say so.
580		if onboarding.AgentsUnwired {
581			fmt.Fprintf(out, "  %-*s %s %s\n", statusLabelWidth, "agents",
582				render.Mark(tui.MarkFailed),
583				render.PhasePaint(tui.PhaseFailed,
584					fmt.Sprintf("not wired — run `%s setup` so your agent uses this brain", brainCmd)))
585			if len(onboarding.AgentsMissing) > 0 {
586				fmt.Fprintf(out, "  %-*s   %s\n", statusLabelWidth, "",
587					render.Dim("missing: "+strings.Join(onboarding.AgentsMissing, ", ")))
588			}
589		}
590		facts := onboarding.Facts
591		factsLine := fmt.Sprintf("  %-*s %s %s distilled",
592			statusLabelWidth, "memories",
593			render.Bar(facts.Distilled, facts.Sessions, statusBarWidth),
594			render.Ratio(facts.Distilled, facts.Sessions))
595		switch {
596		case facts.Running:
597			factsLine += render.PhasePaint(tui.PhaseBackfill, fmt.Sprintf("  (backfill running, pid %d)", facts.PID))
598		case facts.Sessions == 0:
599			factsLine += render.Dim("  (no captured sessions yet)")
600		case facts.Pending() > 0:
601			factsLine += render.Dim(fmt.Sprintf("  (%d pending)", facts.Pending()))
602		}
603		fmt.Fprintln(out, factsLine)
604	
605		daemonPhase := tui.PhaseSkipped
606		daemonMark := tui.MarkSkipped
607		if onboarding.Daemon.Running {
608			daemonPhase, daemonMark = tui.PhaseDaemon, tui.MarkDone
609		}
610		daemonLine := fmt.Sprintf("  %-*s %s %s", statusLabelWidth, "daemon",
611			render.Mark(daemonMark), render.PhasePaint(daemonPhase, describeDaemonState(onboarding.Daemon, brainCmd)))
612		if !onboarding.LastTickAt.IsZero() {
613			age := humanizeAge(report.GeneratedAt.Sub(onboarding.LastTickAt))
614			if onboarding.Daemon.Running {
615				daemonLine += render.Dim(" " + render.Bullet() + " last tick " + age + " ago")
616			} else {
617				daemonLine += render.Dim(" (last watcher tick " + age + " ago)")
618			}
619		}
620		if onboarding.Paused {
621			daemonLine += render.PhasePaint(tui.PhaseSkipped, " "+render.Bullet()+" background work: paused")
622		}
623		fmt.Fprintln(out, daemonLine)
624		// Say what the machine's ONE watcher covers. A hashed launchd label answers
625		// nothing a reader of `status` came to ask; the workspaces it is watching
626		// answer it exactly.
627		if onboarding.Daemon.Installed {
628			if coverage := describeWatchPlanCoverage(onboarding.WatchPlan); coverage != "" {
629				fmt.Fprintf(out, "  %-*s   %s\n", statusLabelWidth, "", render.Dim(coverage))
630			}
631		}
632	
633		if len(onboarding.Components) > 0 {
634			parts := make([]string, 0, len(onboarding.Components))
635			for _, component := range onboarding.Components {
636				mark := setupComponentMark(component.State)
637				phase := tui.PhaseDone
638				switch component.State {
639				case "failed":
640					phase = tui.PhaseFailed
641				case "missing":
642					phase = tui.PhaseSkipped
643				}
644				parts = append(parts, render.Mark(mark)+" "+render.PhasePaint(phase, component.Name))
645			}
646			fmt.Fprintf(out, "  %-*s %s\n", statusLabelWidth, "instant", strings.Join(parts, "  "))
647			// A row of names is not a report. Every failed component already
648			// carries the reason it failed and, for the failure modes whose error
649			// text is not actionable on its own, the hint that fixes it -- status
650			// built both and printed neither, so "x semantic" was the whole answer
651			// and the only way to learn why was to run a different command. Say it
652			// here, under the row that names it, in the same shape setup's own
653			// summary uses.
654			// One remedy, one appearance. Two components failing for the same
655			// reason -- the ordinary case for a dirty worktree, which refuses both
656			// seed and semantic -- carry the same hint, and the verdict below
657			// carries it a third time.
658			said := map[string]bool{strings.TrimSpace(stated): true}
659			for _, component := range onboarding.Components {
660				// A skipped component with a recorded reason reports too — the
661				// reason is the one thing the row's bare glyph cannot say — but
662				// with the skipped glyph and dim phase, because a designed skip
663				// rendered in failure red is the contradiction this distinguishes.
664				skippedWithReason := component.State == "skipped" && strings.TrimSpace(component.Detail) != ""
665				if component.State != "failed" && !skippedWithReason {
666					continue
667				}
668				detail := strings.TrimSpace(component.Detail)
669				if detail == "" {
670					// A failure with no recorded reason is itself worth saying:
671					// silence here would read as "no detail needed".
672					detail = "no reason recorded"
673				}
674				mark, phase := tui.MarkFailed, tui.PhaseFailed
675				if skippedWithReason {
676					mark, phase = tui.MarkSkipped, tui.PhaseSkipped
677				}
678				fmt.Fprintf(out, "  %-*s %s %s\n", statusLabelWidth, "",
679					render.Mark(mark),
680					render.PhasePaint(phase, component.Name+": "+detail))
681				if hint := strings.TrimSpace(component.Hint); hint != "" && !said[hint] {
682					said[hint] = true
683					fmt.Fprintf(out, "  %-*s   %s\n", statusLabelWidth, "", render.Dim("hint: "+hint))
684				}
685			}
686		}
687	}
688	
689	// renderStatusBlindSpotGroups prints one line per collapsed group, and (in
690	// verbose mode) the member paths for the groups that are NOT obvious data.
691	// A data-file group never enumerates: that is the whole point of the collapse,
692	// and `doctor` is where the full list lives.
693	func renderStatusBlindSpotGroups(out io.Writer, render *tui.Renderer, indent string, groups []statusBlindSpotGroup, enumerate bool, brainCmd string) {
694		for _, group := range groups {
695			phase := tui.PhaseSkipped
696			if !group.DataFiles {
697				phase = tui.PhaseFailed
698			}
699			line := group.Summary()
700			if group.DataFiles {
701				line += " " + render.Dash() + " `" + base.SetupBrainCommand(brainCmd) + " doctor` lists them"
702			}
703			fmt.Fprintf(out, "%s%s %s\n", indent, render.Mark(tui.MarkSkipped), render.PhasePaint(phase, line))
704			if !enumerate || group.DataFiles {
705				continue
706			}
707			for _, path := range group.Paths {
708				fmt.Fprintf(out, "%s  %s\n", indent, render.Dim(path))
709			}
710		}
711	}

Recon done. Findings, then a proposed layout for your sign-off.

**What's actually going on:** `brain status` already uses `internal/tui` (same `Renderer` as setup/refresh), and since v0.2.0 the palette is literally copied from the entire CLI (`internal/tui/cli_palette.go`, `styles.go` "default" theme). What doesn't match is the **visual grammar**: the host `entire status` renders `● Enabled · branch x`, dim `·` separators, and yellow `!` warning lines — no bars, no label columns, no glyph-per-component row. Brain status instead has its own layout: an "Onboarding" block, a 14-cell red→amber→green ramp bar (`Renderer.Bar`, `internal/tui/render.go:333` — each cell is colored by position, which is the multicolored graph you're seeing), a color-ramped ratio, and a nine-item `✓ sessions ✓ seed …` row. I checked Brain recall on main: no recorded rationale ties us to the ramp bar.

**Proposed restyle of the default report** (your repo's current data), in the host CLI's grammar:

```
● Brain · gh/entireio/entire-brain
  memories 24,565 · 269/272 distilled (3 pending) · manifest current · Brainstore connected
  daemon not installed · last watcher tick 102h ago
  sources · sessions seed docs history facts patterns entities memory · missing: semantic
  ! no code index · run 'entire brain refresh --agent none'
  ! seed stale · seed and docs are based on an older commit
  Integrity not checked · 'entire brain doctor' for a deep audit · '--verbose' for the full report
```

and when healthy:

```
● Brain · gh/entireio/entire-brain
  memories 24,565 · all distilled · manifest current · Brainstore connected
  daemon running · last tick 3s ago · watching 2 workspaces
  code index · 1,204 files · 18,440 symbols
```

Key moves: the leading dot carries the verdict color (green/yellow/red) like `entire status`'s `● Enabled`; the bar and ramp-colored ratio are gone — plain count instead; the nine-glyph instant row collapses to one line that only names what's missing/failed; problems become `!` lines with their remedy inline, so the separate verdict block disappears. All the existing verdict/remedy logic (`statusHealth`) stays — this is a re-skin of `renderBrainStatusShort` only. `--json` is untouched (golden-test enforced), `--verbose` keeps its current shape, and the live refresh/setup progress bars are out of scope unless you want the ramp gone there too.

Does this layout match what you had in mind — and should the live refresh/setup bars lose the color ramp as well?

we need new lines before and after the main body to give it some space. 

its still very crowded

Agreed — here's a looser cut: blank lines around the body, one fact per line, host-CLI label grammar (`Label · value`, dim labels):

```

● Brain · gh/entireio/entire-brain

  Memories   · 24,565 (269/272 distilled, 3 pending)
  Daemon     · not installed (last watcher tick 102h ago)
  Sources    · sessions, seed, docs, history, facts, patterns, entities, memory
  Manifest   · current
  Brainstore · connected

  ! no code index · run 'entire brain refresh --agent none'
  ! seed stale · seed and docs are based on an older commit

  'entire brain doctor' for a deep audit · '--verbose' for the full report

```

Healthy case:

```

● Brain · gh/entireio/entire-brain

  Memories   · 24,565 (all distilled)
  Daemon     · running (last tick 3s ago, watching 2 workspaces)
  Sources    · sessions, seed, docs, semantic, history, facts, patterns, entities, memory
  Code index · 1,204 files, 18,440 symbols
  Manifest   · current
  Brainstore · connected

  ✓ up to date

```

Structure: header dot carries the verdict color; one blank line after the header, one between the facts block and the `!` warnings, one before the footer. A missing source drops out of the `Sources` line and shows up as its own `!` line instead, so nothing is said twice. Labels and `·` separators are dim, values plain, warnings yellow — exactly `entire status`'s grammar.
